title: Shortest Cut to Leave It Sorted
statement:
You get an integer array arr. You may delete one contiguous stretch of it (possibly empty, possibly the whole array apart from what is kept). What remains, the part before the cut joined to the part after it, must be in non-decreasing order.

Return the length of the shortest stretch you can delete.

examples.why: Cutting [10, 0] leaves [1, 2, 3, 4]. Cutting everything after 10 or everything before 0 would cost 3 each: the best cut keeps part of the front and part of the back.
Strictly falling: at most one value can remain, so three must go.
Equal neighbours are allowed. The array is already sorted.

hints: Whatever you keep is a piece from the front plus a piece from the back. Each of those pieces must already be sorted on its own.
Find the longest sorted prefix and the longest sorted suffix. Cutting off everything after the prefix, or everything before the suffix, is always valid. Can you keep some of both?
Walk a pointer i through the sorted prefix and a pointer j through the sorted suffix. For each i, move j forward until arr[j] ≥ arr[i]; then the cut is j − i − 1. Both pointers only move forward.

explain.intuition:
Deleting one stretch keeps a front piece arr[0..i] and a back piece arr[j..n−1]. Both pieces must be sorted on their own, so the front piece lies inside the longest sorted prefix and the back piece inside the longest sorted suffix. And they must join well: arr[i] ≤ arr[j].

That is a classic two-pointer setup. As i moves right through the prefix, arr[i] only grows, so the first j in the suffix with arr[j] ≥ arr[i] can only move right too. Neither pointer ever goes back, so the whole search is linear. Also count the two one-sided options: keep only the prefix, or keep only the suffix.
steps: Find right, the start of the longest sorted suffix. If it is 0, the array is sorted: return 0.
Set best = right (delete everything before the suffix).
Set j = right. For each i from 0 while the prefix is still sorted (i == 0 or arr[i−1] ≤ arr[i]):
Move j right while j < n and arr[j] < arr[i]. Update best = min(best, j − i − 1). When j = n, that is the cut that keeps only the prefix.
pitfalls: Only trying to remove a whole prefix or a whole suffix. In [1, 2, 10, 0, 3, 4] both cost 3 but the answer is 2.
Treating equal neighbours as a break in order. The order is non-decreasing, so [4, 4] is sorted.
Letting i run past the end of the sorted prefix. Once the prefix breaks, no longer front piece is valid.

solutions.title: Try every cut
solutions.idea: For every start and end of the cut, check whether the remaining values are non-decreasing.

solutions.title: Sorted prefix and suffix, two pointers
solutions.idea: Keep part of the sorted prefix and part of the sorted suffix. As the prefix end moves right, the first suffix position that fits only moves right too.

followups: The remaining array must be strictly increasing. Which comparisons change?
You may delete up to two separate stretches. How does the search change?
